inputs.original_text: Lower courts have ruled school can ban wearing such apparel as ‘can reasonably be interpreted as profane’ The case of two Michigan middle-school brothers who were told to remove their hoodies emblazoned with the phrase “Let’s Go Brandon” is headed to the U.S. Supreme Court. The siblings are represented by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression which says the boys’ school violated their First Amendment rights. The phrase was popularized during a 2021 NASCAR event when a crowd was shouting “F*** Joe Biden!” but the NBC interviewer told racer Brandon Brown they were yelling “Let’s go Brandon!” A judge...
inputs.modified_text: They’re trying to turn a political slogan into “profanity” so schools can suppress it without admitting they’re policing dissent. The phrase’s origin is right there: a crowd was shouting “F*** Joe Biden!” and an NBC interviewer recast it as “Let’s go Brandon!” Now lower courts say schools can ban clothing that “can reasonably be interpreted as profane”—a conveniently elastic rule that lets institutions decide which messages are acceptable. The brothers’ case is headed to the U.S. Supreme Court, and the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression says their First Amendment rights were violated. This looks less like a hoodie dispute than a test of how far officials can stretch a label to silence speech they don’t want heard.
